voiceover: Somewhere in your life, there is a line you know should never be crossed. Torturing a small child for fun. Betraying a friend who trusted you completely. The murder of the innocent. You sense that something is genuinely wrong — wrong even if everyone in the room disagreed, wrong even if a whole nation cheered it on. If someone says they hate cilantro, we shrug. But if someone says cruelty to children is perfectly fine, we think they are mistaken — that they have missed something real. This argument does not say that people who don't believe in God can't be good. They can. The question is: what makes good actually good — for all of us? It can't come only from human opinion, because human opinion changes and disagrees, and yet we sense the wrongness of cruelty doesn't change with the vote. A moral law that stands over all of us, that judges even the majority, looks like something bigger than us. Behind the moral law stands a Lawgiver. Goodness isn't a lonely rule floating in empty space; it is the character of the One who made us. God doesn't invent goodness by decree, and He doesn't consult a rulebook above Himself. God is the good — goodness in person. Every time your conscience insists that something is really wrong, it's pointing past your own preferences toward a goodness that is bigger than you. It may be one of the clearest signals you have that the universe is not cold and blind after all, but the work of a Maker whose very nature is love.
